title: Fisheries Economics
source_note: Standard NUC-aligned Nigerian university 300L Fisheries Economics curriculum: basic economic concepts (demand, supply, cost, revenue, profit) applied to fisheries and aquaculture, the common-property/open-access nature of capture fisheries, production economics of fish farming, fisheries marketing and price formation, and basic investment appraisal for fisheries enterprises. Kept distinct from Fisheries Policy & Legislation (FIS405), which covers law/regulation rather than economic analysis.

questions.question: In basic economics, the 'law of demand' states that, all else being equal:
options: As the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded falls
As the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded also rises
Price has no relationship to quantity demanded
Demand is always fixed regardless of price
questions.correct_answer: As the price of a good rises, the quantity demanded falls
questions.explanation: The law of demand describes an inverse relationship between price and quantity demanded, holding other factors constant, which applies to fish as to other goods.

questions.question: The 'law of supply' states that, all else being equal:
options: As the price of a good rises, the quantity supplied also rises
As the price of a good rises, the quantity supplied falls
Supply is completely unrelated to price
Supply always equals demand at every price
questions.correct_answer: As the price of a good rises, the quantity supplied also rises
questions.explanation: The law of supply describes a direct relationship between price and quantity supplied, as higher prices generally incentivize producers, including fish farmers, to supply more.

questions.question: A fish stock exploited as a common-property (open-access) resource is prone to overexploitation mainly because:
options: No single fisher owns the resource, so individuals have little incentive to limit their own harvest for future benefit
The government automatically restricts all access to zero
Prices for fish are always fixed by law regardless of scarcity
Common property resources cannot be fished at all
questions.correct_answer: No single fisher owns the resource, so individuals have little incentive to limit their own harvest for future benefit
questions.explanation: Because capture fisheries are often open-access common-property resources, individual fishers bear the full benefit of their own catch but share the cost of depletion with all other users, incentivizing overexploitation (the 'tragedy of the commons').

questions.question: The 'tragedy of the commons,' as applied to fisheries, describes a situation where:
options: Individually rational behavior by resource users leads to overexploitation and depletion of a shared resource
A single owner deliberately destroys a resource for personal gain
Open-access resources are always managed sustainably without intervention
Only government-owned resources can ever be overexploited
questions.correct_answer: Individually rational behavior by resource users leads to overexploitation and depletion of a shared resource
questions.explanation: The tragedy of the commons describes how, absent effective management, individually rational decisions to maximize one's own catch collectively lead to overuse and depletion of a shared fishery resource.

questions.question: Total revenue in a fish farming enterprise is calculated as:
options: Quantity of fish sold multiplied by the selling price per unit
Total cost of production minus profit
Fixed cost plus variable cost only
Quantity of feed used multiplied by feed price
questions.correct_answer: Quantity of fish sold multiplied by the selling price per unit
questions.explanation: Total revenue is simply the quantity of output sold multiplied by the price received per unit, a fundamental concept in evaluating any enterprise's financial performance.

questions.question: Fixed costs in a fish farming operation, such as pond construction or land lease, are defined as costs that:
options: Do not vary with the level of output produced in the short run
Change directly and proportionally with production volume
Only occur once a farm has sold all its fish
Are always higher than variable costs
questions.correct_answer: Do not vary with the level of output produced in the short run
questions.explanation: Fixed costs remain constant regardless of production level in the short run (e.g., pond construction, land rent), unlike variable costs such as feed and labor that change with output.

questions.question: Variable costs in a fish farming enterprise, such as feed and fingerlings, are defined as costs that:
options: Change in direct relation to the scale of production
Remain fixed no matter how much fish is produced
Are incurred only after the enterprise closes down
Never appear in a farm's cost accounting
questions.correct_answer: Change in direct relation to the scale of production
questions.explanation: Variable costs, such as feed, fingerlings, and labor tied to stocking levels, rise or fall with the volume of production, unlike fixed costs.

questions.question: Profit in a fish farming enterprise is calculated as:
options: Total revenue minus total cost
Total revenue plus total cost
Fixed cost minus variable cost
Quantity produced divided by price
questions.correct_answer: Total revenue minus total cost
questions.explanation: Profit is the difference between total revenue earned from sales and total cost (fixed plus variable) incurred in production.

questions.question: The break-even point in a fish farming enterprise refers to the level of output or sales at which:
options: Total revenue exactly equals total cost, resulting in zero profit or loss
Profit is at its absolute maximum
The enterprise ceases all operations permanently
Fixed costs become zero
questions.correct_answer: Total revenue exactly equals total cost, resulting in zero profit or loss
questions.explanation: The break-even point is where total revenue equals total cost; below this level the enterprise incurs a loss, and above it the enterprise earns a profit.

questions.question: Economies of scale in fish farming refer to the situation where:
options: Average production cost per unit decreases as the scale of operation increases
Costs rise indefinitely as production increases
Scale of production has no effect on cost per unit
Only small-scale farms can ever be profitable
questions.correct_answer: Average production cost per unit decreases as the scale of operation increases
questions.explanation: Economies of scale occur when expanding production allows a farm to spread fixed costs over more output and gain efficiencies, reducing the average cost per unit produced.

questions.question: Market margin in fish marketing refers to:
options: The difference between the price paid by the final consumer and the price received by the producer/fisher
The total quantity of fish sold in a market
The tax imposed on fish exports only
The cost of fingerlings purchased by a farmer
questions.correct_answer: The difference between the price paid by the final consumer and the price received by the producer/fisher
questions.explanation: Marketing margin captures the gap between the consumer price and the producer (farm-gate) price, reflecting the costs and profits accruing to intermediaries such as transporters, processors, and retailers.

questions.question: Middlemen in the Nigerian fish marketing chain typically perform which economic function?
options: Bulking, transporting, and distributing fish from producers to final consumers or retailers
Directly farming or catching the fish themselves in all cases
Setting the final consumer price by government decree
Eliminating the need for any transportation of fish
questions.correct_answer: Bulking, transporting, and distributing fish from producers to final consumers or retailers
questions.explanation: Middlemen in the marketing chain add value by aggregating small quantities of fish from many producers, transporting them, and distributing them to retailers or consumers, often bridging geographic and scale gaps.

questions.question: Seasonal price fluctuations for fish in Nigerian markets are often driven by:
options: Variations in seasonal catch/harvest volume relative to relatively stable demand
A complete absence of any seasonal variation in fish supply
Fixed government price controls that never change
Consumer preferences that change only once per decade
questions.correct_answer: Variations in seasonal catch/harvest volume relative to relatively stable demand
questions.explanation: Fish supply often varies seasonally (e.g., flood season peaks in inland fisheries, festive demand peaks), and since demand is relatively less variable, these supply shifts drive price fluctuations across the year.

questions.question: Price elasticity of demand for fish measures:
options: How responsive the quantity of fish demanded is to a change in its price
The total volume of fish caught in a season
The exact cost of producing one kilogram of fish
The number of fish species available in a market
questions.correct_answer: How responsive the quantity of fish demanded is to a change in its price
questions.explanation: Price elasticity of demand quantifies the percentage change in quantity demanded resulting from a percentage change in price, helping predict consumer response to price changes.

questions.question: Fish is often considered to have relatively elastic demand in many markets partly because:
options: Consumers can substitute other protein sources (such as meat or eggs) if fish prices rise significantly
There are no substitutes for fish protein anywhere
Fish demand never changes regardless of price
Fish has no nutritional substitutes of any kind
questions.correct_answer: Consumers can substitute other protein sources (such as meat or eggs) if fish prices rise significantly
questions.explanation: Because consumers can often switch to alternative protein sources when fish becomes relatively expensive, demand for fish tends to be price-elastic in many contexts, though this varies by fish type and market.

questions.question: A cost-benefit analysis conducted before investing in a new fish farm is used mainly to:
options: Compare the expected costs and benefits of the investment to assess its economic viability
Determine the exact taxonomic classification of species to be farmed
Replace the need for any technical feasibility study
Set the retail price of fish by government mandate
questions.correct_answer: Compare the expected costs and benefits of the investment to assess its economic viability
questions.explanation: Cost-benefit analysis systematically weighs the anticipated costs against the anticipated benefits of an investment, helping determine whether a fisheries or aquaculture project is likely to be economically worthwhile.

questions.question: The payback period, as an investment appraisal tool for a fish farm, refers to:
options: The length of time required for the investment's net returns to recover the initial capital outlay
The total lifespan of the pond structure
The number of fish harvested in the first cycle
The interest rate charged on a farm loan
questions.correct_answer: The length of time required for the investment's net returns to recover the initial capital outlay
questions.explanation: The payback period measures how long it takes for the cumulative net cash inflows from an investment to equal the original capital invested, a simple tool for assessing investment risk and liquidity.

questions.question: Net Present Value (NPV), a more sophisticated investment appraisal method than payback period, accounts for:
options: The time value of money by discounting future cash flows to their present value
Only the initial capital cost with no future cash flows considered
The exact market price of fish feed only
The taxonomic diversity of species farmed
questions.correct_answer: The time value of money by discounting future cash flows to their present value
questions.explanation: NPV discounts expected future cash inflows and outflows back to present value terms using a chosen discount rate, recognizing that money received in the future is worth less than money received today.

questions.question: Maximum Economic Yield (MEY) in fisheries economics refers to the harvest level at which:
options: The difference between total revenue and total cost of fishing effort is maximized
The maximum possible biological catch is taken, regardless of cost
Total cost of fishing effort is zero
Fish stocks are driven to extinction
questions.correct_answer: The difference between total revenue and total cost of fishing effort is maximized
questions.explanation: MEY is the level of fishing effort/harvest that maximizes net economic profit (total revenue minus total cost), which is generally lower than the effort level that maximizes total biological catch (MSY).

questions.question: Compared to Maximum Sustainable Yield (MSY), Maximum Economic Yield (MEY) is typically achieved at a:
options: Lower level of fishing effort
Higher level of fishing effort
Identical level of fishing effort in all fisheries
Level of effort with no relationship to MSY
questions.correct_answer: Lower level of fishing effort
questions.explanation: Because MEY accounts for the cost of fishing effort, it is generally achieved at a lower effort level than MSY, since beyond MEY, additional effort costs more than the added revenue it generates.

questions.question: Subsidies provided to fishers, such as fuel subsidies, can have the unintended economic effect of:
options: Encouraging excess fishing effort beyond economically or biologically optimal levels
Automatically restoring depleted fish stocks
Eliminating all fishing costs entirely
Having no influence on fishing behavior
questions.correct_answer: Encouraging excess fishing effort beyond economically or biologically optimal levels
questions.explanation: By artificially lowering the cost of fishing, subsidies can incentivize fishers to apply more effort than would be economically rational or biologically sustainable without the subsidy, contributing to overcapacity.

questions.question: Access rights or licensing systems in fisheries management are, from an economic perspective, tools designed mainly to:
options: Limit entry and fishing effort to address the open-access overexploitation problem
Guarantee unlimited access to all fishers with no restriction
Eliminate the need for any market for fish
Set fish prices directly by government decree
questions.correct_answer: Limit entry and fishing effort to address the open-access overexploitation problem
questions.explanation: Licensing and access-rights systems restrict the number of participants or amount of effort in a fishery, aiming to correct the incentive problems inherent in open-access common-property resources.

questions.question: Diminishing marginal returns in fish pond production would be observed if, for example:
options: Each additional unit of feed added beyond a certain point produces progressively smaller increases in fish growth
Every additional unit of feed always produces exactly the same increase in growth indefinitely
Adding feed has no relationship to fish growth at any level
Fish growth increases without limit regardless of feed input
questions.correct_answer: Each additional unit of feed added beyond a certain point produces progressively smaller increases in fish growth
questions.explanation: The law of diminishing marginal returns holds that, beyond some point, adding more of a variable input (like feed) to a fixed resource (like pond space) yields progressively smaller increases in output.

questions.question: A farm-gate price in fish marketing refers to:
options: The price received by the producer at the point of first sale, before intermediary markups
The final retail price paid by the consumer in an urban market
The export price set by international buyers only
The price fixed permanently by government regulation
questions.correct_answer: The price received by the producer at the point of first sale, before intermediary markups
questions.explanation: Farm-gate price is the price a producer (farmer or fisher) receives at the point of initial sale, before transportation, processing, and retail margins are added along the marketing chain.

questions.question: Post-harvest losses in the fish value chain, whether physical or quality-related, represent an economic problem mainly because they:
options: Reduce the marketable output and income from a given amount of fish produced or caught
Automatically increase the total profit of producers
Have no bearing on food security or income
Only occur in aquaculture, never in capture fisheries
questions.correct_answer: Reduce the marketable output and income from a given amount of fish produced or caught
questions.explanation: Post-harvest losses (spoilage, physical damage, quality downgrading) reduce the amount of fish that can be sold or its value, directly lowering the income producers and processors can earn from a given catch or harvest.

questions.question: A cooperative society formed by small-scale fish farmers can provide economic benefits mainly by:
options: Enabling bulk purchase of inputs and collective marketing, improving bargaining power
Automatically eliminating all production risk
Preventing members from selling fish independently under any circumstance
Guaranteeing a fixed government subsidy regardless of performance
questions.correct_answer: Enabling bulk purchase of inputs and collective marketing, improving bargaining power
questions.explanation: Cooperatives allow members to pool resources for bulk input purchase (lowering unit costs) and coordinate marketing/sales, improving their collective bargaining power relative to buyers and input suppliers.

questions.question: Access to credit/finance is often cited as a constraint on small-scale aquaculture development in Nigeria mainly because:
options: Many small-scale farmers lack collateral or credit history required by formal lending institutions
Aquaculture requires no capital investment of any kind
Credit is entirely unnecessary once a farm becomes operational
Formal lenders always readily provide loans to any fish farmer
questions.correct_answer: Many small-scale farmers lack collateral or credit history required by formal lending institutions
questions.explanation: Small-scale fish farmers often lack the collateral, formal records, or credit history that banks and other formal lenders require, limiting their access to the capital needed for farm establishment or expansion.

questions.question: In fisheries economics, 'externalities' refer to:
options: Costs or benefits of an economic activity that fall on third parties not directly involved in the transaction
Only the internal costs recorded in a farm's own accounts
Profits earned exclusively by the government
A term with no relevance to fisheries or aquaculture
questions.correct_answer: Costs or benefits of an economic activity that fall on third parties not directly involved in the transaction
questions.explanation: Externalities are spillover effects, such as pollution from a fish farm harming a downstream water user, that impose costs (or occasionally benefits) on parties outside the original economic transaction.

questions.question: A fish farmer deciding whether to expand production should compare the marginal cost of the expansion to its marginal revenue because profit is maximized where:
options: Marginal cost equals marginal revenue
Total cost is at its absolute lowest regardless of output
Marginal cost is always zero
Total revenue is deliberately minimized
questions.correct_answer: Marginal cost equals marginal revenue
questions.explanation: Standard microeconomic theory holds that profit is maximized at the output level where the cost of producing one more unit (marginal cost) equals the revenue gained from selling that unit (marginal revenue).
